limitations: Participants' 3-back performance was poor, adding noise to the model and potentially obscuring overall interaction effects on the dual n-back task.
Post-environment cognitive testing was conducted on cell phones in distracting lobby/entry areas, which may have negatively impacted performance.
Participants were required to complete multiple surveys on cell phones during their walk, potentially diminishing attention restoration effects.
The study failed to replicate a previously found association between trait impulsivity and increased positive affect in natural environments, possibly due to differences in study design.
The study had less statistical power to observe relationships for individual differences due to these being between-subject analyses.
Participants may have fully explored the study spaces by the end of the one-hour walk, potentially attenuating some observed differences later in the survey.
The duration of the observed differences in affect and thought content after leaving each environment remains unknown.
Technical difficulties prevented participants from taking pictures of visual features during surveys, limiting the ability to compare individualized visual features with thought content.
Participants visited locations without companions, limiting generalizability to social interactions in public spaces.
The study was limited to one natural and one commercial space in a single North American city, potentially limiting the generalizability of findings to other designs, amenities, or cultural contexts.
The chosen locations (conservatory and mall) differ on multiple dimensions beyond naturalness, such as visitor demographics and primary purpose, which could also influence results.
